the main drivers of tropical forest succession are: (i) the level and intensity of disturbance, (ii) the presence of well-preserved native forests in the landscape, (iii) the spatial configuration of forest patches, (iv) the heterogeneity of the landscape matrix and (v) the presence of native forest remnants in the landscape.

the successional pathways of tropical forest stands in human modified landscapes are driven by a combination of factors operating at multiple spatiotemporal scales, and that such factors determine the predictability of successions and the potential of secondary tropical forests to deliver essential ecosystem functions and serve as repositories of biodiversity in HMTL.

secondary forests in human-modified tropical landscapes are a dynamic component of these systems, and their successional pathways depend on a complex set of factors operating at different spatial scales, including landscape spatial configuration, land use history, and matrix heterogeneity.
